The 32 32 selected pairs span the full range of domains, from control and planning to bioinformatics and finance. DocOps ( Jiang et al., 2026a ) . Tasks edit or produce office documents of four types and are organised in tiers of increasing scope: atomic edits of one document, composite operations on one document type, cross-document operations, single-document workflows, and a set of harder publication and repair tasks. Every task injects the skill of its document type ( xlsx , docx , pptx or pdf ), a long reference document with helper scripts such as a LibreOffice recalculation script. The executor runs inside Claude Code; the checker opens the produced document and verifies its realised state, e.g. cell formulas, deleted text spans or theme colours. Of the 32 32 selected pairs, 10 10 are atomic, 10 10 composite, 5 5 cross-document, 1 1 workflow and 6 6 publication or repair tasks. Tessl ( Shaposhnikov et al., 2026 ) . Tasks pair a realistic developer request, e.g. setting up a payment project, configuring tracing or reviewing a cookbook, with a skill published by the tool’s vendor or open-source maintainers, including Stripe, Vercel, ClickHouse, Sentry, Shopify and Firecrawl. The executor runs inside Claude Code, and because these tasks have no single correct artefact, an LLM judge grades the result against a task-specific rubric; we use its normalised score directly. All 39 39 selected pairs are single-skill tasks, each shipping exactly one vendor skill. The two arms of every experiment receive an identical user prompt and differ only in the system prompt ( App. C ). The user prompt contains, in order: (i) the task instruction, declared authoritative for the task, the allowed scope of changes and the delivery path; (ii) the executor interface, i.e. the complete tool list and parameter schema of OpenHands for SkillsBench, or the tool names exposed by Claude Code for DocOps and Tessl, with the note that skill names, file names and section headings are not callable tools; (iii) the current skill, every SKILL.md verbatim, together with the list of auxiliary files in the skill folder; (iv) in the self-evolution setting only, the result of the last attempt ( passed , failed or partial with its score), a step-by-step digest of the executor’s trajectory, and the verifier output; (v) a one-paragraph job statement. In the self-evolution setting the job statement reads “You know what the weak model did, which checks failed, and what the test output said. Rewrite the skill so that the same weak model does better on the next attempt. Do not encode expected values or test-specific answers.”; in the skill adaptation setting, where no execution has taken place, the first sentence is replaced by “Your evidence is the task instruction, the skill as it stands, and the executor’s tool interface.” Output contract. The rewriter returns the complete new contents of every file it changes, one block per file, delimited by <<<FILE path=...>>> and <<<END>>> ; files it does not return are kept unchanged. It may restructure freely: reorder, merge, split or delete what the executor cannot act on. Alternatively it returns a single <<<NO_CHANGE>>> block with a one-line reason and a list of the missing evidence, in which case the executor reruns the unchanged skill. There is no patch format, no required document template and no diagnosis schema; whether to change the skill at all, how much, and in what form is left entirely to the rewriter. Validity checks. The harness applies two checks to each returned file. Loadability : the file must be non-empty, its path must name an existing skill file, its YAML frontmatter must survive with the name field unchanged (the harness registers skills by name), and it must not exceed a 64,000 64{,}000 -character budget, since the skill is injected whole into the executor’s context. Answer leakage : we collect every specific token (identifiers of at least eight characters containing a digit or underscore, and decimals with at least two places) that occurs in the hidden tests or reference solution but neither in the public task material, including the original skill, nor in the evidence shown to the rewriter. A revision that introduces one such expected value, or two such identifiers, is rejected; a token the rewriter could have read in the verifier output is counted but not blocked, since that route is the design of the evidence arm. A response that cannot be parsed is sent back once with the parse error; a loadability or leakage rejection is terminal. When a revision is rejected the executor runs the unchanged skill and the cell is still scored, so invalid rewrites lower the mean of their arm rather than disappearing from it; a NO_CHANGE response is scored in the same way. Scoring conventions. Every model–task–condition cell is run once. Skill adaptation reports the executor’s mean score on the 103 103 pairs under each rewriter. Self-evolution forms a linear chain of five rounds with no selection of the best round and no rollback, and reports each round against a baseline in which the same executor reruns the original skill in the same time window, so that drift of the serving endpoints over the experiment does not enter the gain. Meta-skill (system prompt of the w/ meta-skill arm) Skill Adaptation You are editing one skill — a document that is injected into a coding agent’s context before it starts a task. The agent that will read your output is a small, weak model. It has already tried this task once with the current version of the skill. You are given what happened. Produce a better version. First locate the break, then fix that Across 602 measured model-task cells, weak-model failure sorts into four classes by how far the agent got before it stopped. Read the trajectory and decide which of the four below is the earliest thing that went wrong; a deeper fix has no effect while a shallower break remains. Apply the prescription for that class — edit the passages it implicates, and leave the rest of the document alone. 1. EXE — no action, or errors it never recovered from. One or two tool calls, no file written; it read a format name ( xlsx , pdf ) as if it were a callable tool, or hit an error and stopped. Prescription: near the top, say which names are callable and which are documents, add an environment preflight, and give a fallback for the first likely failure. Give commands the agent can run verbatim. 2. CTX — the skill displaced the task. It succeeded without the skill and failed with it: work went into the skill’s own examples, files it was only asked to patch, or an artefact outside the required path. Prescription: state the user’s task, the allowed modification scope, and the delivery path early, and say in one line that the rest of the document is reference material rather than a new request. If a step needs content from an auxiliary file, inline that content. 3. IF — requirements not met. Files written, plenty of tool calls, and the failed check is a requirement the text already states. It did part of a multi-part requirement and stopped. Prescription: rewrite each implicated requirement as one line of action — target — completion condition , including the negative branch (“if X already exists, stop and change nothing”). Writing more about the requirement does not help; the text was already there. 4. REF — artefact delivered but incorrect. Artefacts complete, requirement covered — and a number, a matrix or a balance that the verifier recomputes differently. It reported a value it never checked. Prescription: add an ending verification step: re-read the artefact from disk, recompute the reported quantity by a second route, compare against an explicit threshold, and loop until it holds. “I wrote the file” and “the run printed no error” are not evidence.
